name: Lake House (under construction)

documented_range.note: THE 1835 GROUNDBREAKING IS NOT ANDREAS. The separately admitted June 10 Chicago Democrat notice establishes an active project before the scene; modern compilations are not the only evidence for this site. chicagology_prefire112 prints an Andreas passage and then two uncredited editorial paragraphs with no typographic break. ANDREAS says: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House, located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter. This hotel, which was built of brick, was three stories and a basement in height, was elegantly furnished throughout, and cost its owners nearly $100,000. ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836.' He gives NO groundbreaking. THE UNCREDITED PARAGRAPH says: 'ground was broken in 1835, and opened in the fall of 1836'. The same paragraph drops Andreas's basement and gives $90,000 against his nearly $100,000, so it is demonstrably not a faithful restatement of the text it sits under, and 'ground broken in 1835' must not be cited as Andreas. data/exclusions.json's lake_house_finished entry sources the 1835 groundbreaking to drloih_hotels, which is a second unfootnoted compilation saying the same thing; two compilations agreeing is not two witnesses. SO: from 1835-01-01, the first day the attested year permits and not a date anybody gives. TO 1836-12-31, a bound at the end of the year the hotel opened - Andreas's 'autumn of 1836' ends this construction state and no source dates the day. WHAT NARROWS THE MIDDLE, and it is the best anchor this record has: J. D. Bonnell, in a letter to the Chicago Times dated 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas, describes arriving in Chicago and walking the town the next morning - 'Passing east, toward the mouth of the river, was THE LAKE HOUSE IN COURSE OF CONSTRUCTION, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball.' Bonnell dates his arrival in the same letter to 'August 25, 1835'. That is eight weeks after the scene date and it is an eyewitness saying the building was visibly going up and not finished. HIS DATE IS NOT CLEAN AND THE CONFLICT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the letter opens 'My first entry into the city of Chicago was forty years ago, August 25, 1835' - forty years before 1876 is 1836 - and Andreas's own lead-in says Bonnell 'came to Chicago in 1837'. The 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836; between 1835 and 1836 the letter's explicit date is preferred. Harriet Martineau, quoted by Andreas from June 1836, still calls it 'a new hotel then building', which is consistent with either. CURRENT EVIDENCE CORRECTION: the earlier ONLY THING wording is superseded by the separate Chicago Democrat notice of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, already cited under function. Its transcription-mediated reading supports an active named project before the scene but no precise groundbreaking day, roof or construction stage. The existing January 1 bound remains inferred, not an observed start date.

position.symbolic_location: North side of the river in Kinzie's Addition, on the block between Kinzie Street and Michigan Street east of Rush Street (today between East Kinzie Street and East Hubbard Street east of North Rush Street), fronting north onto Michigan Street.
position.note: THE THREE STREETS ARE DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS; WHICH SIDE OF RUSH STREET IS NOT DOCUMENTED AT ALL, AND THAT IS WHY THIS POSITION IS CONJECTURAL RATHER THAN INFERRED. Andreas in the hotel chapter: 'located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter'. Andreas in his account of the First Unitarian Society, whose first Chicago service was held in the unfinished building in June 1836: 'The services were held in the Lake House, WHICH STOOD AT THE CORNER OF RUSH AND MICHIGAN STREETS.' Two chapters, one corner, and no side. A block between Kinzie and Michigan has two faces on Rush, about 110 m apart, and nothing reached says which one this is; the east side is adopted because the backers' own ground - Kinzie's Addition - and the north-bank commercial group Bonnell describes east of Rush lie that way, which is an argument about a neighbourhood and not evidence about a building. IF IT IS WRONG THE BUILDING BELONGS ABOUT 110 M WEST. A SECOND AND LARGER TRAP IS IN THE STREET NAME ITSELF. 'Michigan Street' on the north side in 1835 is the east-west street one block north of Kinzie - today's East Hubbard Street - and it is NOT Michigan Avenue, which did not cross the river until 1920. chicagology_prefire112's uncredited paragraph glosses the site as 'near where the Wrigley Building stands today', and the Wrigley Building stands on Michigan AVENUE at the river, about 150 m south-east of the block Andreas's three streets describe and on the wrong side of Kinzie. docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.8 carries the same gloss and additionally renders the third street as 'Michigan (Water)', equating it with North Water Street, which no source reached supports. This record follows Andreas's street names and records the gloss as the error it appears to be. METHOD: the modern East Hubbard Street / North Rush Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 448121.71, N 4637764.21 (OSM node 261149251, fetched 2026-08-11); the building's north face is set on the Michigan Street frontage 12.2 m south of it and its west face on the Rush frontage 12.2 m east of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Michigan Street, which is the one orientation Andreas does state - 'fronting on the latter'. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), plus the block width if the side of Rush is wrong, plus whatever a building site's outline means when the building is not finished. NO SOURCES ARE CITED ON THIS ATTRIBUTE, deliberately: the streets are quoted in this note and are Andreas's, but the COORDINATE turns on a side of Rush Street that no source states, and a citation on a conjectural position would be decorative. THE GROUND UNDER IT IS MODELLED - the e1834_harbor_cut heightfield now runs local E -320..+1700 and N -400..+400, and this footprint at E +1061.2..+1085.2, N +341.2..+356.2 lands on it within the walker's 0.35 m step-up rule, so the phase carries no ground_contact declaration. WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED is the excavation: a construction site is a hole in the ground before it is anything else, and this project has no way to cut a cellar into the terrain, so the shell sits ON the surface rather than in it.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: Reconstructed 24 × 15 m working plan retained from the earlier site. No source supplies a dimension or dated July extent. This is a substantial brick hotel site, bounded by Andreas's later three storeys and basement and nearly $100,000 cost; those facts supply an order of magnitude, not a scale conversion. The entire outline is not walled to one height: the construction_site form gives uneven lifts and material access. A measured contemporary plan or lot conveyance would replace this choice.

kind.note: The magazine selector supplies the existing brick/open-roof family. The construction_site opt-in replaces its uniform magazine walls and painted door with thick, partly raised walls, real work openings and interior timber stages. It makes no claim that this hotel was a magazine. The opt-in is restricted to a one-storey roofless brick worksite and leaves garrison models on their existing builders.

construction.note: THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS STRUCTURE'S FABRIC THAT IS DOCUMENTED, and it is documented in the source's own words: 'This hotel, WHICH WAS BUILT OF BRICK, was three stories and a basement in height' (Andreas, transcribed on chicagology_prefire112, and confirmed in the printed volume). The uncredited paragraph on the same page repeats 'built of brick'. It is also locally plausible rather than merely asserted: Tyler K. Blodgett established Chicago's first brickyard on the North Side in the spring of 1833 (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.12; data/structures/brickyard_north_side.json). NOTE WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED BY IT: that any brick had been laid by 1835-07-01. Andreas describes the FINISHED hotel of 1836. The material is carried into the scene-date shell as an inference about continuity of intention, which is a small step and still a step.

period_brick.note: T-3387: laid in K03's lake-clay brick (`soft_mud_salmon_lake`): Chicago's own first brick, from Blodgett's North Side yard of 1833, which the record traces this building's brick to; the local lake clay is high in lime and burns salmon to buff, not red. The shade, the bond and that the Lake House's brick came from that yard's clay are the reconstruction (L-k03-period-brick-3387).

stories.note: One partially raised working storey is a reconstructed July 1835 choice within a zero-to-two-storey range, not a measured schedule. The 10 June notice attests active work; Bonnell retrospectively describes construction under a conflicting 1835/1836/1837 date, Martineau describes unfinished work in June 1836, and Andreas gives an autumn 1836 opening. These bound an unfinished project but cannot select the July lift. The model chooses one incomplete lift without a roof or completed-hotel fittings.

wall_height_m.note: The maximum working-front wall is 4.0 m; other lifts step down to 1.2–3.28 m. These are reconstructed bounds inherited from the earlier four-metre shell, not measured basement or storey heights. The worksite remains below the later three-storey completed hotel, and no uniform four-metre enclosure is implied.

roof_type.note: Reconstructed open-shell choice for 1 July 1835. The 10 June notice establishes work before the scene but dates no roof or lift. Neither the June 1836 unfinished interior nor autumn opening proves July roof absence. Roof none omits all caps; the worksite is built openly at the reconstructed tier. The later Kellogg print shows a completed roof and cupola in ca.1836–1849 and is ineligible to prescribe the July construction stage.

paint.note: The archetype's `paint` names the wall's surface finish, not a coat of paint, and 'brick' is the value that lets the documented brick fabric read as brick. It is inferred rather than documented because nothing describes the surface of this building at any date: bare brick is the ordinary finish and the alternative - stuccoed or whitewashed - is not excluded by anything, though it would be an odd thing to do to an unfinished shell.

chimneys.note: NOT A COUNT OF THE FINISHED HOTEL'S STACKS, which nobody records, but a consequence of the state: a shell one storey up has no chimneys standing above it. The archetype places stacks against the ridge, and this structure has no ridge. Inferred from the construction state rather than from any statement.

construction_site.note: A bounded July 1835 worksite, not a reconstruction of the completed hotel. The 10 June Chicago Democrat notice establishes a house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. No source measures the July progress. Within the existing 24 × 15 m plan and 4 m maximum, 0.46 m thick brick walls now step down from the higher north working front to the lower rear lift. Seven selected work bays have real unglazed openings and only the first three have their brickwork bridged above reconstructed timber lintels; a broad rear break admits material. Two short timber working stages stand inside the shell. Bay count, wall thickness, lift heights, apertures, staging stock and placement are reconstructed working choices, not features traced from the later print. The existing external brick, timber and footing-stone piles remain separately declared in the yard layer. No excavation or below-grade interior is represented. L-lake-house-worksite-2379.

phases.change_note: On 1 July 1835 this is an active hotel-building project, attested by the 10 June notice. Its particular stage is reconstructed: an uneven, roofless brick lift with open work bays and two internal timber stages, on the existing 24 × 15 m plan at a 4 m maximum. No completed-hotel roof, cupola, glazing, sign or accommodation is backdated from the later image.

function.note:
The building's purpose is documented and its completion date is documented, and between them they make the scene-date function a construction site rather than a hotel. Andreas: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836, Jacob Russel, of Middleton, Conn., assuming control of its management.' The men behind it are documented too and are worth carrying because they are the town's commercial leadership rather than innkeepers: Gurdon S. Hubbard, General David S. Hunter, John H. Kinzie, Dr W. B. Egan and Major James B. Campbell - 'the men whose enterprise led them into building a house which for those days was far in advance of the needs of the town'.

AND THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS DATES THE SITE, WHICH ANDREAS DOES NOT. 'There is [a] new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake Hous[e]."' — the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, the same paragraph that reports the Sauganash freshly refitted. Both halves are load-bearing. IT IS A BUILDING SITE three weeks before the scene date, north of the main branch, which is what makes hotel_under_construction an attested function at 1835-07-01 rather than a back-projection from the 1836 opening. AND ITS NAME IS STILL SECOND-HAND — 'we understand' — so on the scene date the town has an unfinished building that people are calling the Lake House and not a hotel with a sign. The same paragraph contains an editorial proposal for a house 'about double the size of that latter' near the centre of Lake Street on this side of the river. The comparison expresses a desired relative hotel size; it supplies no measured dimensions or July construction stage and does not establish the Lake House's rank among existing buildings. The proposal is not an existing-house observation and does not prove that the suggested site was vacant.

Fergus's 1876 recollection of the 1839 hotel is included here only for later establishment identity and the conflicting Rush/North Water address, not as evidence of the July 1835 construction stage, position or dimensions. Its Hotels entry was directly checked at the printed page; the existing contemporary project notice remains the evidence for work before the scene date.

research_note:
The Lake House was building before this scene: the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reports a new house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. The held newspaper reading is transcription-mediated, with bracketed supplies; no original facsimile was newly read. Andreas says the completed hotel was brick, three storeys and a basement, and opened in autumn 1836.

LIBERTIES: No source dates its precise progress on 1 July. The scene chooses an incomplete, roofless working lift: stepped brick walls, seven selected work bays, open apertures and two internal timber stages. The 24 × 15 m extent, four-metre maximum, masonry thickness, smaller lifts and staging are reconstructed. Brick, timber and footing stone beside it are the existing reconstructed yard layer. No below-grade cellar is depicted. The open shell represents one bounded choice within the retained zero-to-two-storey uncertainty; that uncertainty does not require an empty site.

THE PICTURE SHOWS A LATER STATE: kellogg_blanchard_1856_old_fort_lake_house is the public-domain 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print, misleadingly stored under an 1830 filename. Its labelled Lake House has a completed roof, cupola and three window rows in a scene of about 1836–1849. It is linked as later context and does not attest this July stage. No completed-state geometric match or July picture is claimed. The duplicate planning image is the same composition; Milwaukee's Lake House is a different hotel. The source page also carries an about-1860 completed-hotel photograph and an 1869 map, plus two later text-ad/menu images; none depicts July progress.

SITING: The existing reconstructed position follows Andreas's Kinzie/Rush/Michigan account and the north-side Michigan Street reading (today Hubbard), with about twenty metres of survey uncertainty and an unresolved side-of-Rush choice. Fergus's 1839 address recalled in 1876 instead prints Rush and North Water. The source page's 1869 map places the later hotel west of Rush, contradicting the existing reconstructed east-side choice. This is recorded as a later mapped-state conflict, without asserting that the later plan measures this July worksite. That later conflict does not justify moving the July site to the modern Wrigley gloss. Bonnell's date conflict remains recorded in the research dossier. The source/date coverage and finite worksite acceptance are in docs/RESEARCH/lake-house-completion-20261110/README.md.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS 51 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.
